profiles.meeting_scenario: At a university-affiliated academic medical center, the Office of Human Research Protections is holding a design review of a draft 'Ethical Quality Review Scorecard' that would be piloted alongside standard IRB review for investigator-initiated studies. The draft scorecard is intended to help the institution move beyond checking procedural compliance and assess whether protocol review meaningfully addresses Belmont-related concerns such as welfare, respect, and justice. The immediate agenda is to review version 0.8 of the scorecard, decide whether it is ready for a six-month pilot, and identify revisions to the reviewer guidance memo and reporting template. The expected outcome is a conditional go-ahead for pilot preparation, with agreed edits to the scorecard package and a shared sense that the tool is 'ready' for committee use.

members.name: Elena Morales
members.role: Associate General Counsel for Research Compliance
members.expertise: Research regulation, IRB governance, federal human subjects requirements, institutional policy drafting
members.background: Elena is a former hospital compliance attorney who now advises the medical center's HRPP and IRBs on Common Rule interpretation, consent documentation, and oversight risk. She regularly translates federal guidance into institutional review checklists and has been asked to help make sure the new scorecard can survive external scrutiny.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot approved quickly but in a form that can be defended if regulators, accreditors, or plaintiff's counsel later ask how the institution evaluated ethical review quality. She is especially concerned about creating a document that looks like a binding legal standard or exposes the institution by recording unresolved ethical criticism too bluntly.
hidden_assumptions: If a review tool is described as 'for the pilot,' it should be limited to the convened IRB's protocol-level deliberation and not expand into auditing recruitment conduct, post-approval monitoring, or investigator behavior.
A scorecard is 'ready' once reviewers can apply it consistently enough to produce a defensible institutional record, even if the scoring guidance is still somewhat high-level.

The 'justice' section will naturally be evaluated from what appears in the submitted protocol and consent materials, because IRBs are not positioned to judge broader community access conditions beyond the file.

When discussing the 'recent suspension cases,' everyone is referring to federal shutdowns driven by compliance findings at major academic centers, which are the relevant cautionary precedent for tool design.

members.name: Dr. Marcus Liu
members.expertise: Bioethics, empirical assessment of IRB performance, reviewer training, human subjects protection program evaluation
members.background: Marcus is a PhD bioethicist who previously led quality-improvement studies on consent comprehension and participant burden in multisite trials. He was asked to champion the scorecard because he has argued publicly that procedural compliance metrics miss whether review actually promotes respect, welfare, and justice.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot to preserve the aspirational ethical purpose of the project rather than letting it collapse into another compliance instrument. He is worried that if the scorecard is narrowed too much, the institution will claim success without learning whether IRB review improves participant-facing ethics.
hidden_assumptions: If a review tool is 'for the pilot,' it should test whether the institution's oversight process as a whole advances participant protection, including issues that emerge in recruitment plans, community-facing materials, and implementation feedback.

A scorecard is 'ready' once it is conceptually faithful to Belmont principles and useful for reflective improvement, even if inter-rater reliability and documentation conventions are still being refined during the pilot.

The 'justice' section should prompt reviewers to consider whether the study's access, burden distribution, and exclusions are fair in practice, including likely effects on populations who never appear in the formal protocol packet.

When discussing the 'recent suspension cases,' the relevant lessons include not just federal compliance shutdowns but also the publicized subject deaths and advisory-body critiques showing that rule-following can miss deeper ethical failures.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the pilot's scope
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the scorecard should evaluate 'ethical quality of IRB oversight' during the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means assessment of the quality of the IRB committee's review of the protocol file before approval, using only materials already in the board packet.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means assessment of whether the institution's oversight process actually surfaces and improves participant-facing ethical issues across review, recruitment planning, and early implementation feedback.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In this domain, 'IRB oversight' naturally sounds broad but respectable, and both participants support the same high-level reform goal, so neither pauses to mark the operational boundary.

misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats 'justice' as whether the inclusion/exclusion criteria and subject selection rationale documented in the protocol are not facially inappropriate or inconsistent with regulations and institutional policy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats 'justice' as whether the study fairly distributes burdens and access in the real enrollment environment, including language access, recruitment reach, and practical barriers for underrepresented groups.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The Belmont term is familiar to both, creating strong false consensus; because both can cite subject selection as an example, the difference between document-based fairness and real-world access remains submerged.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes the tool 'ready' for pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both ask whether version 0.8 is 'ready' and whether reviewer guidance is 'enough for the pilot.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes readiness means the tool has sufficiently stable anchors, documentation language, and reviewer instructions to yield a consistent and defensible record across committees from day one.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes readiness means the tool is mature enough to begin iterative learning, with the expectation that ambiguity and variation will be discovered and corrected during the six-month pilot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Pilot projects routinely tolerate imperfection, and both parties expect revision later, so the phrase 'ready for pilot' sounds aligned even though one assumes near-operational standardization and the other assumes exploratory refinement.

misalignment_points.topic: Which cautionary precedent they are designing against
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the suspension cases' and 'what happened at the major centers' as justification for the scorecard design.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking primarily of federally imposed research suspensions triggered by documented regulatory noncompliance at academic medical centers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the broader cluster of events commonly discussed together: subject deaths, public criticism, and advisory reports arguing that compliant IRBs may still miss ethically important problems.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The historical episodes are often bundled together in institutional memory and policy discussions, so a shorthand reference to 'the suspension cases' feels precise enough even though each person is anchoring on a different subset of events.

turns.inner_thought: What I need from this meeting is a clean decision that version 0.8 is ready for the pilot in the practical sense: stable enough that different reviewers can use it without producing wildly inconsistent records, and careful enough that if OHRP, an accreditor, or plaintiff's counsel ever asks how we assessed ethical review quality, the institution can show a disciplined process. I am fine with refining later, but I do not want to launch something that reads like an aspirational essay rather than an operational tool.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. I thought we could use today to answer two fairly concrete questions: first, whether version 0.8 is ready for a six-month pilot, and second, whether the scorecard package as a whole is credible as an institutional review tool. For me that means looking not just at the domains, but also at the guidance memo and reporting template, so we know committees can use it in a disciplined way.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this from becoming another procedural score sheet. The point of the pilot is to see whether ethical quality of IRB oversight is actually being captured in a way that reflects participant-facing ethics across the oversight process, not just whether a committee can fill out a form against the packet. If we lose that, the institution will claim improvement without learning anything important.
turns.utterance: I agree. And I would just underline that the pilot should really test ethical quality of IRB oversight, not simply layer on another compliance checklist. If reviewers can use the scorecard to notice whether our oversight is surfacing the right ethical issues, then the pilot is doing useful work.

turns.inner_thought: The draft is workable because the convened IRB already has what it needs in the protocol file and board materials to assess respect, welfare, and justice at the review stage. We should not imply the pilot is auditing downstream conduct or institutional access conditions. Justice, in this context, should be judged from the documented inclusion and exclusion plan, subject selection rationale, and consent language already before the board.
turns.utterance: Looking at the current draft, I do think the core domains are there. The board packet already gives reviewers enough material to assess respect, welfare, and justice in a disciplined way, provided the prompts are framed clearly enough. So my instinct is that we are not missing whole domains so much as tightening how reviewers are asked to apply them.

turns.inner_thought: Justice is still too abstract. If we don't include examples that point reviewers toward what participation will actually feel like and who may be left out in practice, they'll default to the formal selection section and miss the real ethical issue. I can still say this in language Elena will hear as strengthening the domain without forcing the scope disagreement into the open.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. On the draft itself, I think the justice domain would benefit from a few more concrete examples. Right now it reads correctly in principle, but reviewers may need prompts that bring it down to things like language accessibility, transportation burden, and whether recruitment channels systematically miss certain communities.

turns.inner_thought: I'm happy to add examples under justice, but they need to stay anchored to what the committee can actually review from the file and discuss in the meeting. I do not want a tool that invites commentary on facts outside the submission or creates a record of criticisms the IRB was never in a position to verify. Keep it tied to eligibility criteria, enrollment plans, and consent documents.
turns.utterance: I agree that justice needs clearer examples. I would just want those examples tied closely to what reviewers can actually see and evaluate consistently—for example, eligibility criteria, enrollment targets, and consent language already in the protocol file. That will keep the domain usable across committees.

turns.inner_thought: This is exactly the lesson from the suspension cases as I understand them: formal review can look complete while ethically significant participant harms or exclusions go unseen. The major-center failures were not just about missing a citation requirement; they showed how rule-following can coexist with deeper failures. I should invoke that shared institutional memory because Elena will also accept the cautionary frame, even if she's thinking of a narrower set of events.
turns.utterance: Right, and to me that was exactly the lesson from the suspension cases and what happened at the major centers. The procedural review could look complete on paper, and still important ethical concerns were not really being surfaced. That is part of why this scorecard matters.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and those federal shutdowns are precisely why I want tighter anchors and careful memo language. If we are ever asked how this institution evaluated ethical review quality, we need to show a consistent process, not an open-ended set of impressions. The scorecard cannot become an invitation to document unresolved criticisms in a way that looks like the institution knew of defects but lacked standards.
turns.utterance: I don't disagree, and those suspension cases are also why I want the scoring anchors and the memo language to be tight. If this tool is ever questioned later, the institution needs to be able to show that reviewers were using a consistent process rather than free-form impressions. So some of this is about making the record sturdy.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with some ambiguity at launch. For me, ready for the pilot means mature enough to start learning from use, not polished enough to operate like a settled compliance instrument on day one. What I most want is evidence about where current oversight fails to surface ethical concerns; the pilot is the mechanism for discovering that.
turns.utterance: Consistency matters, absolutely. At the same time, for the pilot, what I most want is for reviewers to start using the tool and generate insight about where ethical concerns are not being surfaced now. If version 0.8 is enough for the pilot in that sense, we can learn a lot even before everything is fully refined.

turns.inner_thought: I need to put a boundary around this now without making it sound restrictive. The safest way is to define the worksheet around materials already in ordinary convened IRB review: protocol file and committee discussion notes. That keeps the pilot within standard workflows and avoids drift into recruitment conduct, implementation issues, or investigator behavior outside the board's immediate review record.
turns.utterance: One practical adjustment I would suggest, then, is that the reviewer worksheet be limited to protocol materials and committee discussion notes. That would keep the pilot aligned with normal IRB oversight workflows and make it easier for committees to incorporate the scorecard without building a separate process around it.

turns.inner_thought: I can accept that as the basic structure if I preserve a bridge to the broader oversight questions I care about. The reporting template should still note whether recruitment or participant-facing implementation concerns were identified for follow-up, so we don't collapse oversight into the packet alone. That phrasing should sound compatible enough to Elena.
turns.utterance: That works for me as a starting structure. I would still like the reporting template to capture whether recruitment and participant-facing implementation concerns were identified for follow-up, so the pilot tells us something about the ethical quality of IRB oversight rather than only whether the worksheet was completed.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with that if it's framed carefully and doesn't turn the scorecard into a record of unbounded institutional criticism. We seem close enough to call this ready: add a few examples under justice, clean up the scoring guidance, and preserve disciplined language. That is sufficient for pilot preparation from my standpoint.
turns.utterance: I think that's manageable if we phrase it carefully. So, from where I sit, with a few clarifying examples under justice and some cleaner scoring guidance, version 0.8 sounds ready to move into pilot preparation. I would treat today's edits as tightening the package rather than reopening the whole design.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I have enough to move forward, and I still believe the pilot can test whether oversight is ethically meaningful beyond compliance if I shape the examples and memo thoughtfully. Elena thinks we're stabilizing a defensible committee-use tool; I think we're launching an exploratory ethics-improvement instrument. As long as both of us say it's ready, the pilot can start.
turns.utterance: That sounds right to me. I'll revise the examples in the justice domain and tune the guidance memo so reviewers have enough structure for the pilot, while still letting us test whether oversight is ethically meaningful beyond compliance. If we do that, I think we can begin pilot prep on schedule.
